# Introduction

This project was my final assignment for a university course in *Longitudinal
and Survival Data Analysis*. The dataset is simulated; my course instructor
provided it.

The study has **240 patients** with a chronic disease. Each patient received
either the **standard treatment** (`treatment = 0`) or a **new treatment**
(`treatment = 1`).

- A **biomarker** was measured four times: at the start (month 0) and at 3, 6 and 12 months.
- Patients were then followed for up to seven years to see whether they **died**.

I answer two questions:

1. **Does the biomarker change over time, and does the change differ between the two treatments?**
2. **Do patients on the new treatment live longer?**

```{r packages}
library(tidyverse)  # reading, reshaping and plotting data
library(lme4)       # linear mixed model
library(lmerTest)   # p-values for the mixed model
library(survival)   # Kaplan-Meier, log-rank test and Cox model
```

# Data

```{r read}
data_wide <- read.table("data/extra_data.txt", header = TRUE)
head(data_wide)
```

| Variable | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `id` | patient number |
| `treatment` | 0 = standard, 1 = new |
| `age` | age in years |
| `sex` | 0 = female, 1 = male |
| `bio_0`, `bio_3`, `bio_6`, `bio_12` | biomarker at month 0, 3, 6 and 12 |
| `follow` | follow-up time in years |
| `death` | 1 = died, 0 = still alive at the end of follow-up (censored) |

The data have **one row per patient**. For the longitudinal model I need
**one row per measurement**, so I reshape the data from wide to long format.

```{r long}
data_long <- data_wide |>
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("bio_"),
               names_to = "visit", values_to = "biomarker") |>
  mutate(month = as.numeric(sub("bio_", "", visit)),
         group = factor(treatment, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("Standard", "New")))

head(data_long)
nrow(data_long)   # 240 patients x 4 visits = 960 rows
```

# Part 1: How does the biomarker change over time?

## Plot

Each thin line is one patient. The thick lines are the average of each group.

```{r trajectories}
group_means <- data_long |>
  group_by(group, month) |>
  summarise(biomarker = mean(biomarker))

ggplot(data_long, aes(x = month, y = biomarker, colour = group)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = id), alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_line(data = group_means, linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_point(data = group_means, size = 3) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 3, 6, 12)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Standard" = "#2C7FB8", "New" = "#D95F0E")) +
  labs(x = "Month", y = "Biomarker", colour = "Treatment",
       title = "Biomarker over 12 months") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r means-table}
group_means |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = month, values_from = biomarker, names_prefix = "Month ") |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1)
```

The biomarker goes down in both groups, and it goes down faster in the
new-treatment group. The plot also shows that some patients are always high
and others always low, so measurements from the same patient are related.

## Linear mixed model

A normal regression assumes every row is independent. Here each patient has
four measurements, so they are not independent. A **linear mixed model with a
random intercept** handles this by giving each patient their own starting
level.

The model is:

> biomarker = time + treatment + time × treatment + (a random starting level for each patient)

The **time × treatment** term tests whether the biomarker changes at a
different speed in the two groups.

```{r lmm}
model <- lmer(biomarker ~ month * treatment + (1 | id), data = data_long)
summary(model)
```

```{r lmm-ci}
confint(model, parm = "beta_", method = "Wald")
```

**What the results mean**

- **`month` (about −0.90):** with the standard treatment, the biomarker goes down by about 0.9 units every month.
- **`month:treatment` (about −0.56, p < 0.001):** with the new treatment, it goes down about 0.56 units *faster* per month, so about 1.46 units per month in total. After 12 months that is roughly 6.7 units more decrease than with the standard treatment.
- **`treatment` (about −3.7):** the new-treatment group already started about 3.7 units lower at month 0. This is a difference between the groups at the start, not an effect of the treatment.
- **Random effects:** the variance between patients (`id`) is larger than the leftover variance (`Residual`). Most of the variation comes from patients being different from each other, which is why a mixed model is needed.

# Part 2: Do patients on the new treatment live longer?

## Kaplan–Meier curves

The Kaplan–Meier method estimates the probability of still being alive at each
point in time. It also handles patients who were still alive at the end of
follow-up (censored).

```{r km}
km <- survfit(Surv(follow, death) ~ treatment, data = data_wide)
km
```

```{r kaplan-meier}
plot(km, col = c("#2C7FB8", "#D95F0E"), lwd = 2, mark.time = TRUE,
     xlab = "Years", ylab = "Probability of survival",
     main = "Kaplan–Meier survival curves")
legend("bottomleft", legend = c("Standard", "New"),
       col = c("#2C7FB8", "#D95F0E"), lwd = 2)
```

```{r km-3years}
summary(km, times = 3)
```

The new-treatment curve stays above the standard curve during the whole
follow-up. After 3 years about **73%** of the new-treatment patients are still
alive, compared with about **57%** of the standard-treatment patients.

## Log-rank test

The log-rank test checks whether the two survival curves are statistically different.

```{r logrank}
survdiff(Surv(follow, death) ~ treatment, data = data_wide)
```

The p-value is **0.009**, which is below 0.05. The survival curves of the two
groups are significantly different.

## Cox proportional hazards model

The log-rank test does not adjust for other variables. The **Cox model**
estimates the effect of treatment while taking **age** and **sex** into
account. The result is a **hazard ratio (HR)**:

- HR < 1: lower risk of death
- HR = 1: no difference
- HR > 1: higher risk of death

```{r cox}
cox <- coxph(Surv(follow, death) ~ treatment + age + sex, data = data_wide)
summary(cox)
```

**What the results mean**

- **Treatment: HR = 0.56 (95% CI 0.36 to 0.87, p = 0.01).** Patients on the new treatment have about **44% lower risk of death** than patients on the standard treatment of the same age and sex.
- **Age: HR = 1.03.** Each extra year of age increases the risk of death by about 3%.
- **Sex: HR = 1.13, p = 0.6.** There is no clear difference between men and women.

### Checking the proportional hazards assumption

The Cox model assumes that the hazard ratio stays the same over time. The
`cox.zph()` function tests this. A p-value **above 0.05** means the assumption is OK.

```{r ph-check}
cox.zph(cox)
```

All p-values are above 0.05, so the assumption holds.

# Conclusions

1. **Biomarker:** the biomarker decreases over time in both groups, and it decreases faster with the new treatment (about 1.46 vs 0.90 units per month).
2. **Survival:** patients on the new treatment live longer. The Kaplan–Meier curves and the log-rank test (p = 0.009) show a clear difference.
3. **Cox model:** after adjusting for age and sex, the new treatment lowers the risk of death by about 44% (HR 0.56).

**Limitation:** the data are simulated, so the results only show how these
methods work. They say nothing about a real treatment.
